Chapter 3: The Body as a Site of Public Scrutiny and Private Pain
Let’s talk about what it really feels like to move through the world in a body that others see as different. It’s not just something out there—it’s both public and deeply personal, all at once.
Picture this: you’re out for a jog, and you feel those eyes following you. Or you step into an upscale boutique, and suddenly, you can just sense suspicion hanging in the air. Even in places that should feel safe, your body can become a battleground of tension and awareness.
Now, here’s something to pay attention to—not all of this scrutiny comes from the outside. Over time, it creeps in. You start to anticipate the looks, the questions, the judgments. Shoulders tense up, your posture shifts, every movement gets a little more careful. It’s almost like you’re performing—trying to blend in, aiming to seem non-threatening, hoping not to stand out. But no matter what you do, it feels like you can’t really escape notice.
Sometimes, that scrutiny turns harsh—even hostile. Maybe you’re pulled over while driving, and the situation escalates for no clear reason. Or you’re a teenager, just shopping, but suddenly you’re being followed and accused of theft with zero evidence. These moments aren’t just rare exceptions—they’re part of a bigger pattern. A constant reminder that, for some, the body always feels exposed, always at risk.
All this takes a real toll on the mind and spirit. Anxiety settles in, humming quietly in the background of every day. Sleep gets restless, dreams turn uneasy. Even if you try to move forward, your body keeps carrying the weight of these experiences.
But here’s the other side—your body isn’t just a target. It’s also a source of joy and strength. Think about those moments when you’re laughing with friends or dancing at a party. In those times, you feel free, unburdened. These flashes of happiness are precious, a reminder that your body is so much more than a site of pain—it’s also about pleasure and connection.
Still, the line between public and private is thin. The pain from public moments seeps into private ones, shaping how you see yourself and how you relate to others. Maybe a parent’s worried about their child’s safety, teaching them how to move through a world that isn’t always gentle. Or a partner offers comfort, but that underlying fear just won’t let go.
And then there’s the way art and media shape this whole dynamic. Images of violence against Black bodies get shared over and over, often stripped of context or care. Some folks get desensitized, while others are retraumatized, again and again. The body becomes a symbol, even a spectacle—its real humanity gets lost in a story about threat and danger.
So, what do we do in the face of all this? There’s a deep need to reclaim the body—to say, “Yes, I belong. I’m valuable. I have the right to exist without fear.” That act of reclamation? It’s resistance. It’s refusing to let others define your worth.
And maybe the most powerful thing to remember is this: despite everything, the body endures.
